## Stochastic modeling solutions

These solutions use the shared root environment and keep the checks close to
the model code.  Seeds make the example output reproducible, but they do not
turn stochastic results into universal constants.

### Continuous-time Markov chains and jump processes

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-ch04-ex1}

The two infectious stages use rate $2\gamma$.  Their sum is an Erlang
distribution with mean $2/(2\gamma)=1/\gamma$, matching the original
single-stage mean, but variance $2/(2\gamma)^2=1/(2\gamma^2)$, half the
single exponential variance.

```{julia}
using Catalyst
using JumpProcesses
using StableRNGs

N, β, c, γ = 1000, 0.05, 10.0, 0.25
κ = β * c / N
network = @reaction_network begin
    κ, S + I₁ --> 2I₁
    2γ, I₁ --> I₂
    2γ, I₂ --> R
end

u₀ = [:S => 990, :I₁ => 10, :I₂ => 0, :R => 0]
problem = JumpProblem(
    network, u₀, (0.0, 40.0), [:κ => κ, :γ => γ];
    aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(20250711),
)
solution = solve(problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = 0.2)
states = Array(solution)
mass_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(states; dims = 1)) .- N))
nonnegative = minimum(states) >= 0
integer_valued = all(x -> isapprox(x, round(x)), states)
@assert mass_error == 0
@assert nonnegative && integer_valued
(; mass_error, nonnegative, integer_valued)
```

The infection propensity remains $\kappa SI_1$; the second infectious
compartment only changes the recovery path.  The conservation check is exact
because every reaction removes one individual from one compartment and adds
one to another.  Compared with one exponential infectious period, the
two-stage construction reduces unrealistically short and long durations while
preserving the mean.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-ch04-ex2}

For a pure birth--death count $Z$, a `DiscreteProblem` and two
`ConstantRateJump`s are sufficient.  The death affect function guards the
boundary; its constant rate is a deliberately simple toy approximation.

```{julia}
using JumpProcesses
using StableRNGs

function birth!(integrator)
    integrator.u[1] += 1
end
function death!(integrator)
    integrator.u[1] = max(integrator.u[1] - 1, 0)
end

toy = DiscreteProblem([5], (0.0, 20.0), nothing)
birth_rate(u, p, t) = 0.8
death_rate(u, p, t) = 0.8
birth_jump = ConstantRateJump(birth_rate, birth!)
death_jump = ConstantRateJump(death_rate, death!)
toy_problem = JumpProblem(
    toy, Direct(), birth_jump, death_jump;
    rng = StableRNG(20250712),
)
toy_solution = solve(toy_problem, SSAStepper())
@assert minimum(reduce(vcat, toy_solution.u)) >= 0
```

To add vaccination to SIR, introduce the transition $S\to R$ with
propensity $a_{\mathrm{vac}}=\nu S$.  A state-dependent propensity is a
`VariableRateJump`:

```{julia}
function infection!(integrator)
    integrator.u[1] -= 1
    integrator.u[2] += 1
end
function recovery!(integrator)
    integrator.u[2] -= 1
    integrator.u[3] += 1
end
function vaccinate!(integrator)
    integrator.u[1] -= 1
    integrator.u[3] += 1
end

ν = 0.01
sir = DiscreteProblem([990, 10, 0], (0.0, 40.0), nothing)
jumps = (
    VariableRateJump(
        (u, p, t) -> κ*u[1]*u[2], infection!;
        urate = (u, p, t) -> 125.0,
        rateinterval = (u, p, t) -> 40.0,
    ),
    VariableRateJump(
        (u, p, t) -> γ*u[2], recovery!;
        urate = (u, p, t) -> 250.0,
        rateinterval = (u, p, t) -> 40.0,
    ),
    VariableRateJump(
        (u, p, t) -> ν*u[1], vaccinate!;
        urate = (u, p, t) -> 10.0,
        rateinterval = (u, p, t) -> 40.0,
    ),
)
vaccinated_problem = JumpProblem(
    sir, Coevolve(), jumps...;
    dep_graph = [[1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]],
    rng = StableRNG(20250713),
)
vaccinated_solution = solve(vaccinated_problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = 0.2)
vaccinated_states = Array(vaccinated_solution)
@assert maximum(abs.(vec(sum(vaccinated_states; dims = 1)) .- 1000)) == 0
```

The mean-field equations become
$$
\dot S=-\kappa SI-\nu S,\quad
\dot I=\kappa SI-\gamma I,\quad
\dot R=\gamma I+\nu S.
$$

If $\nu$ depends on calendar time, the rate is no longer constant.  A
`VariableRateJump` with a time argument (as above) is appropriate, or the
process can be simulated in pieces over intervals on which the campaign rate
is constant.

### Stochastic differential equations

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-ch05-ex1}

The experiment keeps the model, seed, and output grid fixed while changing the
Euler--Maruyama step.  Conservation is a property of the reaction-level noise,
whereas nonnegativity is not guaranteed by any finite `dt`.

```{julia}
using StochasticDiffEq
using StableRNGs

N, β, c, γ = 1000.0, 0.05, 10.0, 0.25
κ = β * c / N
u₀ = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]

function f!(du, u, p, t)
    κ, γ = p
    a₁ = κ * max(u[1], 0.0) * max(u[2], 0.0)
    a₂ = γ * max(u[2], 0.0)
    du[1], du[2], du[3] = -a₁, a₁ - a₂, a₂
end
function g!(G, u, p, t)
    κ, γ = p
    a₁ = κ * max(u[1], 0.0) * max(u[2], 0.0)
    a₂ = γ * max(u[2], 0.0)
    s₁, s₂ = sqrt(a₁), sqrt(a₂)
    G[1, 1], G[2, 1], G[3, 1] = -s₁, s₁, 0.0
    G[1, 2], G[2, 2], G[3, 2] = 0.0, -s₂, s₂
end

function run_sde(dt)
    problem = SDEProblem(
        f!, g!, u₀, (0.0, 30.0), (κ, γ);
        noise_rate_prototype = zeros(3, 2),
    )
    solution = solve(
        problem, LambaEM();
        dt, adaptive = false, saveat = 0.1,
        rng = StableRNG(20250711),
    )
    states = Array(solution)
    (
        dt = dt,
        conservation_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(states; dims = 1)) .- N)),
        minimum_state = minimum(states),
    )
end

results = run_sde.( (0.1, 0.05, 0.01) )
@assert all(result.conservation_error < 1e-8 for result in results)
results
```

Reducing `dt` reduces discretization error and usually makes boundary
crossing less frequent, but a Gaussian increment has unbounded support for
every positive step size.  A negative value can therefore still occur.  If
nonnegativity is essential, use the integer CTMC or a method with an explicit
nonnegative boundary treatment rather than silently clipping the output.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-ch05-ex2}

Independent state noise has a diagonal $3\times3$ diffusion.  The comparison
below uses the same drift and seed as the reaction-level SDE.

```{julia}
using StochasticDiffEq
using StableRNGs

function diagonal_g!(G, u, p, t)
    κ, γ = p
    a₁ = κ * max(u[1], 0.0) * max(u[2], 0.0)
    a₂ = γ * max(u[2], 0.0)
    fill!(G, 0.0)
    G[1, 1] = sqrt(a₁)
    G[2, 2] = sqrt(a₁ + a₂)
    G[3, 3] = sqrt(a₂)
end

reaction_problem = SDEProblem(
    f!, g!, u₀, (0.0, 30.0), (κ, γ);
    noise_rate_prototype = zeros(3, 2),
)
diagonal_problem = SDEProblem(
    f!, diagonal_g!, u₀, (0.0, 30.0), (κ, γ);
    noise_rate_prototype = zeros(3, 3),
)
reaction_solution = solve(
    reaction_problem, LambaEM();
    dt = 0.02, adaptive = false, saveat = 0.1,
    rng = StableRNG(20250711),
)
diagonal_solution = solve(
    diagonal_problem, LambaEM();
    dt = 0.02, adaptive = false, saveat = 0.1,
    rng = StableRNG(20250711),
)
reaction_states, diagonal_states = Array(reaction_solution), Array(diagonal_solution)
reaction_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(reaction_states; dims = 1)) .- 1000))
diagonal_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(diagonal_states; dims = 1)) .- 1000))
(; reaction_error, diagonal_error,
    infected_difference = maximum(abs.(reaction_states[2, :] .- diagonal_states[2, :])))
```

For the reaction model $Q=GG^\mathsf{T}$ has
$$
Q_{12}=Q_{21}=-a_1,\qquad Q_{23}=Q_{32}=-a_2,\qquad Q_{13}=0.
$$

The diagonal model sets all off-diagonal covariances to zero.  It also gives
the total $S+I+R$ a nonzero noise term, so its conservation error is not a
roundoff diagnostic.  Its infected trajectory is a different stochastic
model, not merely a noisier numerical solve.

### Agent-based models

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-ch06-ex1}

The grid model changes the contact assumption: a susceptible samples only
agents in its Moore neighborhood.  `nearby_agents` excludes the focal agent,
and `GridSpace` supplies positions through the Agents.jl 7 `@agent` API.

```{julia}
using Agents
using Distributions
using Statistics
using StableRNGs

@agent struct GridPerson(GridAgent{2})
    status::Symbol
    next_status::Symbol
end

function grid_agent_step!(person, model)
    person.next_status = person.status
    if person.status == :S
        neighbors = collect(nearby_agents(person, model, 1))
        k = rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt))
        for _ in 1:k
            isempty(neighbors) && break
            contact = rand(abmrng(model), neighbors)
            if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β
                person.next_status = :I
                break
            end
        end
    elseif person.status == :I &&
           rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt)
        person.next_status = :R
    end
end

function grid_model_step!(model)
    for person in allagents(model)
        person.status = person.next_status
    end
end

space = GridSpace((20, 20); periodic = false)
grid_S(model) = count(p.status == :S for p in allagents(model))
grid_I(model) = count(p.status == :I for p in allagents(model))
grid_R(model) = count(p.status == :R for p in allagents(model))
model = StandardABM(
    GridPerson, space;
    agent_step! = grid_agent_step!,
    model_step! = grid_model_step!,
    properties = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, Δt = 0.1),
    rng = StableRNG(20250714),
)
for id in 1:200
    position = (rand(abmrng(model), 1:20), rand(abmrng(model), 1:20))
    status = id <= 5 ? :I : :S
    add_agent!(position, model; status, next_status = status)
end
_, data = run!(
    model,     200;
    mdata = [grid_S, grid_I, grid_R],
    showprogress = false,
)
counts = Matrix(data[:, [:grid_S, :grid_I, :grid_R]])'
@assert maximum(abs.(vec(sum(counts; dims = 1)) .- 200)) == 0
```

The well-mixed derivation no longer applies: contacts are not uniform over all
$N$ agents, and the infection probability depends on local occupancy and
boundary effects.  Conservation still holds because the update changes status
but never creates or removes an agent.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-ch06-ex2}

The physical horizon is held at 30 time units, so each run uses
`round(Int, 30 / Δt)` updates.  A small seeded ensemble reports the peak
distribution for each timestep.

```{julia}
@agent struct Person(NoSpaceAgent)
    status::Symbol
    next_status::Symbol
end

function agent_step!(person, model)
    person.next_status = person.status
    if person.status == :S
        for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt))
            contact = random_agent(model)
            if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β
                person.next_status = :I
                break
            end
        end
    elseif person.status == :I &&
           rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt)
        person.next_status = :R
    end
end

function model_step!(model)
    for person in allagents(model)
        person.status = person.next_status
    end
end

infected_count(model) = count(p.status == :I for p in allagents(model))

function initialize_gridless(seed, Δt, nsteps)
    model = StandardABM(
        Person;
        agent_step!,
        model_step!,
        properties = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, Δt = Δt),
        rng = StableRNG(seed),
    )
    for id in 1:200
        status = id <= 5 ? :I : :S
        add_agent!(Person(; id, status, next_status = status), model)
    end
    _, data = run!(
        model, nsteps;
        mdata = [infected_count],
        showprogress = false,
    )
    return collect(data.infected_count)
end

summaries = map((0.2, 0.1, 0.05)) do Δt
    peaks = [
        maximum(initialize_gridless(5000 + replicate, Δt, round(Int, 30 / Δt)))
        for replicate in 1:16
    ]
    (; Δt, mean_peak = mean(peaks), sd_peak = std(peaks))
end
summaries
```

The output is a distribution over realizations, not a single deterministic
peak.  Changing $\Delta t$ changes both the numerical update frequency and
the discrete-time biological interpretation: the contact and recovery
probabilities are recalculated at a different interval.  Therefore timestep
sensitivity is not purely a solver error study.  A useful reference is the
continuous-time SIR ODE peak, but agreement is expected only as the
well-mixed, small-step approximation becomes appropriate.
